newsitem.title: USA: Perry tells Clinton he plans to resign - officials.
newsitem.headline: Perry tells Clinton he plans to resign - officials.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry has told President Bill Clinton he plans to resign his Cabinet post, perhaps within a few months, U.S. defence officials said on Wednesday.

One official, who asked not to be identified, said Perry told his staff early on Wednesday he informed Clinton after the president's re-election that he wanted to return to private life after nearly three years on the job.
The news that Perry, 69, planned to leave came on the heels of statements by State Department officials that Secretary of State Warren Christopher planned to resign his post within days.

Perry told his staff he had set no definite date for leaving and expected to stay on for at least a few months until Clinton appointed a successor. Perry took the job in 1994 after the late Defence Secretary Les Aspin resigned under pressure.

There was no immediate indication who might succeed Perry, but published reports have speculated that CIA Director John Deutch and retiring Georgia Sen. Sam Nunn are among the top candidates. And Deputy Attorney General Jamie Gorelick, who previously served as the Pentagon's top lawyer, has made no secret of her desire for the job.

Despite thorny military questions about the continuing role of U.S. military peacekeepers in Bosnia and responsibility for two bomb blasts in Saudi Arabia that killed more than 20 U.S. soldiers, Perry is considered by many experts to be one of the strongest and most popular defence secretaries in decades.
But he has followed a work and travel schedule that would have left many less active people exhausted.

"I don't think there is any good time or bad time walking away from the job as secretary of defence," Perry told reporters three weeks ago while returning from a trip to Europe. "There is always a problem. There is always a crisis. There's always some programme that is halfway completed."

"I should, for point of reference, say that I had not decided to take this job in the first place. It was not something I sought, something I was anxious to do," Perry said. "It was something which was urged on me and after a lot of consideration I finally decided to do."

Perry, in response to questions at the time, expressed some pride in initiatives the Pentagon had taken under him. These included sharply cutting Cold War nuclear weapons in the United States and the former Soviet Union, improving support for military personnel and dependents, and reforming the way the Pentagon buys arms and equipment to save billions of dollars.

"Whenever I leave the Defence Department, I would like to be able to look back and say first of all I have done something significant and, secondly, many of the long-term programmes that I have worked on will continue long after I leave," he said.
